newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS sees growth in asset-backed securities.
newsitem.headline: BIS sees growth in asset-backed securities.

text.p: Securities backed by assets have grown strongly in volume this year and could more than triple in volume in 1996 compared with last year, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Wednesday.
The BIS, central bank to the world's central banks, said in a quarterly report on global financial markets that new issues of asset-backed securities could total some $90 billion this year.

It added it believed the market would expand further in coming years as regulatory barriers fall and competitive pressures induce financial institutions to attach greater importance to increasing return on capital.
In a review of the first nine months of 1996, the BIS said the U.S. dollar accounted for 80 percent of total issuance, followed at a considerable distance by sterling with six percent.
It said that although diversification outside these two currencies has been limited so far, deals have nevertheless been denominated in several other currencies.

There has been evidence of diversification away from U.S. and U.K. originators, with structures arranged for a growing number of continental European issuers, including the first deals for a German non-financial firm.
The report noted that such instruments have also been introduced in Asia, most notably for borrowers from China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan and Thailand.
Non-mortgage assets accounted for over 83 percent of international issuance in the first three quarters of the year.

Of the $67.3 billion of asset-backed securities launched in the international market over that period, issues backed by credit card receivables represented more than 40 percent, or $29.1 billion, followed by mortgage-related issues with $11.5 billion, bonds backed by automobile leases with $8.1 billion and student loan structures, with a volume of $6.8 billion.

The remaining $11.8 billion consisted of issues backed by a variety of assets such as outstanding high-yielding developed and developing country securities and foreign currency receivables under structures established by Latin American securitisation vehicles.
Others included second mortgages, aircraft leases, consumer and corporate loans, and a unique Spanish issue related to the country's nuclear industry.
